timeline.change: Launched in August 1965 as a roadster (U13), half-cab (U14) and wagon (U15) with the 105 hp 170 six, column-shift three-speed and Dana 20. The 289 V8 arrives in March 1966. 23,776 sold
Sport package, dual master cylinder with split brakes, self-adjusting brakes, optional 11.5-gal auxiliary tank
Locking front hubs, revised bumpers and side-marker reflectors. Last year of the roadster
302 V8 replaces the 289; electric wipers replace vacuum ones midyear; steering stabilizer standard
Evaporative emissions controls and smaller fuel tanks. The Sport becomes a separate model
Dana 44 front axle replaces the Dana 30 midyear. Baja Bronco package introduced
Ranger trim arrives; last year of the half-cab; fuel tanks reduced again
C4 automatic and power steering optional; 200 six replaces the 170; J-shift Dana 20 with a 2.34:1 low range from midyear
California-specific emissions equipment; best sales year at 25,824
Catalytic converter and unleaded fuel. CJ Pony Parts lists the 302 at 125 hp net
Power front disc brakes, larger rear drums, front anti-roll bar, quicker steering box (about four turns lock to lock) and a Y-type steering linkage that Autotrader Classics says was poorly received
Heavy-duty 9-inch rear housing, fuel doors instead of exposed caps, 14.4-gal plastic main tank and 8-gal auxiliary. Last year before the full-size Bronco

identify.intro: Most early Broncos have been modified, re-engined or re-bodied, and some are built on reproduction bodies and aftermarket frames. The frame VIN and the glovebox data plate are your starting points.

items.head: VIN layout
items.body: Eleven characters, such as U15GL followed by six serial digits. Positions 1–3 are the series: U13 roadster, U14 half-cab pickup, U15 wagon. Position 4 is the engine: F for the 170 six, S for the 200 six, N for the 289 and G for the 302. Position 5 is the plant, L for Michigan Truck. The model year is worked out from the serial range.

items.head: Where to look
items.body: The VIN is stamped on the frame rail under the engine, just ahead of the firewall; with the wheel turned fully right it can be seen from the wheel well. The full data plate is inside the glovebox door, with codes for paint, body, transmission, axle and sales district.

items.head: Axle code
items.body: The data plate's axle code gives the ratio and whether there's a limited-slip: CJ Pony's 1968 decoder lists 3.50, 4.11 and 4.57 ratios, with separate codes for the limited-slip versions. On the truck itself, the Dana 30 front has king pins and the Dana 44 has ball joints.

items.head: Transfer-case shifter
items.body: A straight up-and-down T-handle means a 1966–72 Dana 20 with a 2.46:1 low. A backward-J pattern means a 1973–77 case with 2.34:1. Rebuild parts differ between them.

items.head: Front brakes and steering
items.body: Factory front discs and a Y-type tie rod mean 1976–77 hardware. Earlier trucks with discs have been converted. Many trucks of every year now carry aftermarket steering linkage.

items.head: Special editions
items.body: Baja Broncos (650 sold) and other high-value trucks are worth faking, and the VIN alone won't prove one. Ask for build documentation and get a marque specialist to inspect it.

capability.note: Capacities varied by year; an 11.5-gal auxiliary tank was optional from 1967

values.intro: Values roughly doubled between 2016 and 2019 and kept climbing, but Hagerty recorded a 12 percent drop in the second quarter of 2026. Who built the truck now matters more than the year.
values.note: Based on 306 complete early Broncos sold on Bring a Trailer, August 2025–October 2026 (middle-half ranges). The median stock or mildly modified truck sold for about $55.5k. Baja Broncos sold for $72.5k–178.3k, and ICON BR builds for $233k–240k. Hagerty says a driver-grade truck still costs $50,000 or more.

production.intro: Ford built about 225,600 early Broncos at the Michigan Truck Plant in Wayne, Michigan, over 12 model years.

editions.name: Roadster (U13)
editions.note: Doorless open body, the cheapest Bronco; dropped after 1968 for lack of sales.

editions.name: Half-cab pickup (U14)
editions.note: Popular with fire and towing operators; dropped after 1972.

editions.name: Sport
editions.note: Chrome trim, wheel covers and red-painted FORD grille lettering.

editions.name: Baja Bronco
editions.note: Designed by Bill Stroppe and sold through Ford dealers: automatic, quick-ratio power steering, flares, Gates Commando tires, roll bar, tricolor paint. $5,566 new; 650 sold.

editions.name: Ranger
editions.note: Top trim with body stripes, cloth seats, woodgrain door panels and carpet.
